questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
? ÷ 9 − 14 × 3 = 1,008 ÷ 24 + 5 × 7

solution.concept: Finish × and ÷ on both sides first, then undo the operations on ? in reverse order
solution.why_others_wrong: 315 subtracts 42 from 77 instead of adding it (35 × 9); 693 forgets the − 14 × 3 term (77 × 9); 1,197 divides 1,008 by 18 instead of 24 (56 + 35 + 42 = 133, × 9).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
?% of 640 + 18² = 7 × 68

solution.concept: Evaluate the known terms, isolate the percentage term, then convert: ?% of 640 = ? × 6.4
solution.why_others_wrong: 125 adds 324 instead of subtracting it (800 ÷ 6.4); 74.375 ignores the 18² term (476 ÷ 6.4); 2.375 divides by 64 instead of 6.4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
2¾ + 3⅚ − 1⅝ = ?

solution.concept: Add and subtract the whole parts and the fractional parts separately, using the LCM 24 for the fractions
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 5/24 adds 1⅝ instead of subtracting it; 6 5/24 subtracts only the whole 1 and adds the ⅝; 3 23/24 subtracts 2 in the whole parts instead of 1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
0.36 × 2.5 + 4.8 ÷ 0.12 − 1.9 = ?

solution.concept: Do × and ÷ before + and −; to divide by a decimal, multiply both numbers by a power of 10
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 takes 4.8 ÷ 0.12 as 4 (dividing by 1.2); 399 takes it as 400 (dividing by 0.012); 42.8 adds the 1.9 instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
√0.0169 + √1.69 + √169 = ?

solution.concept: The square root of a decimal has half as many decimal places: √0.0169 = 0.13, √1.69 = 1.3
solution.why_others_wrong: 15.6 takes √0.0169 as 1.3; 13.26 takes √1.69 as 0.13; 1.443 misplaces the decimal point in the sum.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
(√12 + √27 − √48)² = ?

solution.concept: Write each surd as a multiple of the same surd (here √3) before adding or subtracting
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 takes √48 as 3√3, leaving 2√3; 27 takes √48 as 2√3, leaving 3√3; 243 adds √48 instead of subtracting it (9√3, squared).

solution.concept: Recognise the identity a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)²
solution.explanation: With a = 2.75 and b = 1.25 the expression is (a + b)² = (2.75 + 1.25)² = 4² = 16.
solution.shortcut: Spot the pattern a² + 2ab + b² instead of multiplying the decimals out.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.125 adds only the two squares and drops the 2ab term; 4 forgets to square a + b; 2.25 uses (a − b)² = 1.5².

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the value of (2¹⁰ − 2⁸) ÷ (2⁷ + 2⁶)?

solution.concept: Take the smallest power out as a common factor in the numerator and in the denominator
solution.explanation: Numerator: 2⁸(2² − 1) = 2⁸ × 3. Denominator: 2⁶(2 + 1) = 2⁶ × 3. So the value is 2⁸ ÷ 2⁶ = 2² = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 divides 768 by 2⁷ alone; 12 divides it by 2⁶ alone; 2 subtracts the exponents inside each bracket (2¹⁰⁻⁸ ÷ 2⁷⁻⁶), which is not allowed for a sum or difference.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 4ˣ − 4ˣ⁻¹ = 24, what is the value of (2x)ˣ?

solution.concept: Take the smaller power out as a factor: 4ˣ − 4ˣ⁻¹ = 4ˣ⁻¹(4 − 1); then write both sides as powers of 2
solution.why_others_wrong: 216 rounds the solution to x = 3 (6³); 25 drops the half power and takes 5²; 3√3 solves 2x = 3 (forgetting the − 2), so x = 1.5 and 3^1.5 = 3√3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the value of √0.444… + √2.777… + √0.111…, where each decimal has its last digit recurring.

solution.concept: Convert each recurring decimal to a fraction with denominator 9 (0.ddd… = d/9), then take square roots
solution.why_others_wrong: 3⅓ adds the fractions 4/9 + 25/9 + 1/9 and forgets the square roots; 2⅓ converts 2.777… as 1 + 7/9 = 16/9 (root 4/3); 8/9 takes the roots of the numerators but forgets that √9 = 3 in the denominator.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
∛4912.7 × 5.97 + √728.6 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round to the nearest perfect cube and square: 4913 = 17³ and 729 = 27²
solution.why_others_wrong: 102 stops before adding √728.6; 75 subtracts the 27 instead of adding it; 139 is 10 away from the exact value (about 128.5).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
?% of 1599.7 ≈ 16.98² − 34.96% of 140.2

solution.concept: Round, finish the right side, then ?% of 1600 = 16 × ?
solution.explanation: 17² = 289 and 35% of 140 = 49, so the right side ≈ 240. Then ?% of 1600 = 240 gives ? = 240 ÷ 16 = 15.
solution.why_others_wrong: 21 adds 49 instead of subtracting it (338 ÷ 16 ≈ 21); 18 ignores the 35% term (289 ÷ 16 ≈ 18); 9 is 6 away from the exact value (about 15.0).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
√5183.9 × ∛0.3429 ≈ ?

solution.concept: 5184 = 72²; the cube root of a decimal with three decimal places has one: ∛0.343 = 0.7
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.04 takes ∛0.343 as 0.07; 504 takes it as 7; 64.8 takes it as 0.9.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(8.97 × 13.02 + 2.99 × 13.01) ÷ 5.98 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round, then take the common factor 13 out of the bracket
solution.why_others_wrong: 156 forgets to divide by 5.98; 13 divides by 12 instead of 6; 20 multiplies only the first 9 by 13 ((117 + 3) ÷ 6).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
0.4998 × ? + 1/0.0499 ≈ 61.97

solution.concept: 1/0.05 = 20; then undo the + and the × in reverse order
solution.why_others_wrong: 21 multiplies 42 by 0.5 instead of dividing; 164 adds 20 instead of subtracting it; 120 takes 1/0.05 as 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(? + 14.98% of 239.9) ÷ 6.02 ≈ 27.03 × 3.99 − √1023.6

solution.concept: Finish the right side, multiply back by 6, then remove the known part of the bracket
solution.why_others_wrong: 492 adds 36 instead of subtracting it; 456 is the value of the whole bracket, not of ?; 612 forgets the √1024 term (108 × 6 − 36).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
?² + √4095.7 × 2.99 ≈ 24.02² + 3.98² (? is positive)

solution.concept: Round each term, isolate ?², then take the positive square root
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 keeps only the 24.02² term; 28 adds 192 instead of subtracting it (√784); 400 is ?², not ?.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
50, 61, 58, 69, 66, ?

solution.concept: The steps alternate: + 11, − 3, + 11, − 3, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 63 applies − 3 again instead of + 11; 74 adds the net change of a pair of steps (+ 8); 88 adds 11 twice.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
4, 7, 11, 18, ?, 47, 76

solution.concept: Each term is the sum of the two terms before it
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 repeats the difference 7; 36 doubles 18; 22 adds the first difference 4 again. None of them gives 47 at the next step (18 + 25 = 43, 18 + 36 = 54, 18 + 22 = 40).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
81, 27, 54, 18, 36, 12, ?

solution.concept: The operations alternate: ÷ 3, × 2, ÷ 3, × 2, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 divides by 3 again; 36 repeats the previous high term; 6 halves 12 instead of doubling it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
100, 132, 148, 156, 160, ?

solution.concept: The differences halve each time: 32, 16, 8, 4, …
solution.explanation: The differences are 32, 16, 8, 4, so the next difference is 2 and the term is 160 + 2 = 162.
solution.why_others_wrong: 164 adds 4 again; 161 halves twice and adds 1; 158 subtracts 2 instead of adding it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
3, 4, 13, 38, 87, ?

solution.concept: The differences are the squares of odd numbers: 1², 3², 5², 7², …
solution.explanation: The differences are 1, 9, 25, 49 = 1², 3², 5², 7². The next is 9² = 81, so the term is 87 + 81 = 168.
solution.why_others_wrong: 151 adds 8², an even square; 136 adds 7² again; 187 adds 10², skipping 9².

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
3, 15, 35, ?, 99, 143

solution.concept: Each term is the product of two consecutive odd numbers: 1 × 3, 3 × 5, 5 × 7, …
solution.explanation: 3 = 1 × 3, 15 = 3 × 5, 35 = 5 × 7, so the missing term is 7 × 9 = 63; then 9 × 11 = 99 and 11 × 13 = 143. (Equivalently each term is one less than an even square: 4 − 1, 16 − 1, 36 − 1, 64 − 1, …)
solution.why_others_wrong: 55 adds 20 again; 64 is 8² and forgets the − 1; 48 is 7² − 1, the pattern applied to an odd base.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
2, 3, 10, 15, 26, 35, ?

solution.concept: Odd positions are n² + 1 and even positions are n² − 1
solution.shortcut: Differences 1, 7, 5, 11, 9 alternate between two series rising by 4: the next difference is 15.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 uses 7² − 1, the even-position rule; 49 forgets the ± 1 altogether; 44 adds 9 again.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
256, 320, 400, 500, 625, ?

solution.concept: Each term = previous term × 1.25 (= 5/4)
solution.why_others_wrong: 750 adds the last difference 125 again; 812.5 multiplies by 1.3; 1,250 doubles 625.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 2, 2, 4, 8, 32, ?

solution.concept: Each term is the product of the two terms before it
solution.why_others_wrong: 64 only doubles 32; 128 multiplies 32 by 4 instead of 8; 1,024 squares 32.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
5, 6, 4, 8, 0, 16, ?

solution.concept: The differences are +1, −2, +4, −8, +16: they double in size and alternate in sign
solution.explanation: Differences: +1, −2, +4, −8, +16. The next difference is −32, so the term is 16 − 32 = −16.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 adds 32 and ignores the alternating sign; 0 subtracts 16, repeating the size of the last step; −48 doubles the step twice (− 64).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
5, 10, 26, 50, 122, ?

solution.concept: Each term is (a prime number)² + 1, taking the primes in order: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 145 uses 12, which is not prime; 290 uses 17 and skips 13; 226 uses 15, which is not prime.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
4, 9, 25, 64, 169, ?

solution.concept: Take square roots: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 — each is the sum of the two before it
solution.explanation: √ of the terms: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. Each is the sum of the previous two (2 + 3 = 5, 3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 8 = 13), so the next root is 8 + 13 = 21 and the term is 21² = 441.
steps: Rule: add the two previous roots
solution.why_others_wrong: 289 = 17² takes the roots as primes (2, 3, 5, … but 8 is not prime); 324 = 18² adds 5 to 13, repeating an earlier gap; 338 doubles 169.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 3, 10, 29, 74, ?

solution.concept: Each term = previous term × 2 + a perfect square, the squares rising 1², 2², 3², …
solution.why_others_wrong: 164 adds 16 again; 148 only doubles; 223 uses × 3 + 1, which fits only the step 3 → 10.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
2, 7, 23, 47, 119, 167, ?

solution.concept: Add 2 to each term: 4, 9, 25, 49, 121, 169 are the squares of consecutive primes
solution.explanation: Each term is p² − 2 for the primes p = 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. The next prime is 17, so the term is 17² − 2 = 287.
solution.why_others_wrong: 223 uses 15 and 254 uses 16, neither of which is prime; 359 uses 19 and skips 17.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
2, 3, 8, ?, 3968

solution.why_others_wrong: 48 multiplies 8 by 6; 65 uses 8² + 1; 24 multiplies 8 by 3. None of them gives 3968 at the next step (48² − 1 = 2303, 65² − 1 = 4224, 24² − 1 = 575).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve equations I and II and choose the relation between x and y that is true for every pair of their roots.
I. x² − 19x + 90 = 0
II. y² − 13y + 40 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise each quadratic; compare the smallest x with the largest y
solution.explanation: I: (x − 9)(x − 10) = 0, so x = 9 or 10. II: (y − 5)(y − 8) = 0, so y = 5 or 8. The smallest x (9) is greater than the largest y (8), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y come from a sign slip that gives negative roots for I (−9 and −10).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Work out the roots of both equations, then mark the relation between x and y.
I. x² + 5x − 84 = 0
II. y² − 16y + 63 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: When the two equations share a root, the relation can only be non-strict
solution.explanation: I: (x + 12)(x − 7) = 0, so x = 7 or −12. II: (y − 7)(y − 9) = 0, so y = 7 or 9. x = 7 = y is possible, and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
steps: Other pairs: x < y ⇒ x ≤ y
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses the common root 7; x ≥ y holds only for the pair x = y = 7.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Both equations have only negative roots. Solve them and choose how x is related to y.
I. x² + 18x + 80 = 0
II. y² + 11y + 30 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: With all coefficients positive, both roots are negative; compare the largest x with the smallest y
solution.explanation: I: (x + 8)(x + 10) = 0, so x = −8 or −10. II: (y + 5)(y + 6) = 0, so y = −5 or −6. The largest x (−8) is below the smallest y (−6), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y come from comparing 8 and 10 with 5 and 6 without the minus signs.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find all the roots of I and II and decide which relation between x and y, if any, always holds.
I. 2x² − 11x + 12 = 0
II. y² − 7y + 10 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: If the roots of one equation lie on both sides of a root of the other, no relation holds for every pair
solution.explanation: I: (2x − 3)(x − 4) = 0, so x = 1.5 or 4. II: (y − 2)(y − 5) = 0, so y = 2 or 5. x = 4 is above y = 2 but below y = 5, so the relationship cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y uses only the pair x = 4, y = 2; x ≤ y and x < y use x = 1.5 or the pair x = 4, y = 5.
solution.final_answer: Option A: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is linear with decimal coefficients and equation II is quadratic. Solve both and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 0.4x + 1.2 = 0.25x + 2.1
II. y² − 13y + 42 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Collect the x-terms in the linear equation; a value shared with the quadratic makes the relation non-strict
solution.explanation: I: 0.4x − 0.25x = 2.1 − 1.2, so 0.15x = 0.9 and x = 6. II: (y − 6)(y − 7) = 0, so y = 6 or 7. x = y when y = 6 and x < y when y = 7, so x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses y = 6; x > y comes from moving 1.2 to the right side with the wrong sign (0.15x = 3.3 ⇒ x = 22).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations, whose roots are fractions, and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 6x² − 19x + 15 = 0
II. 10y² − 29y + 21 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Split the middle term using factors of a × c; check for a common root
solution.explanation: I: 6x² − 9x − 10x + 15 = (2x − 3)(3x − 5) = 0, so x = 1.5 or 5/3. II: 10y² − 15y − 14y + 21 = (2y − 3)(5y − 7) = 0, so y = 1.5 or 1.4. x = y = 1.5 is possible and every other pair has x > y, so x ≥ y.
steps: Other pairs: x > y ⇒ x ≥ y
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y misses the common root 1.5; x < y comes from taking 5y − 7 = 0 as y = 7/2 = 3.5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is a perfect square. Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 4x² + 12x + 9 = 0
II. y² + 3y + 2 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: A perfect-square quadratic has one repeated root; see where it falls among the other equation's roots
solution.explanation: I: (2x + 3)² = 0, so x = −1.5 only. II: (y + 1)(y + 2) = 0, so y = −1 or −2. −1.5 lies between −2 and −1: it is greater than −2 but less than −1. So the relationship cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y compares −1.5 with −2 only; x ≤ y and x < y compare it with −1 only.
solution.final_answer: Option A: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is an exponential equation. Find every real value of x and y and choose the relation between them.
I. 2^(x²) = 16ˣ
II. y² − 9y + 20 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Write both sides with base 2 and equate the exponents; do not divide by x, which could be zero
solution.explanation: I: 16ˣ = 2^(4x), so x² = 4x, i.e. x(x − 4) = 0 and x = 0 or 4. II: (y − 4)(y − 5) = 0, so y = 4 or 5. x = 4 = y is possible and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
steps: x = y = 4 possible; else x < y
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses the common value 4; x ≥ y holds only for x = y = 4, and dividing by x (losing x = 0) still leaves x = 4 < 5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I contains fractions in x (x ≠ 0, −1). Clear them, solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 3/x + 4/(x + 1) = 2
II. 4y² − 8y + 3 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Multiply through by x(x + 1) to get a quadratic; check that the roots do not make a denominator zero
solution.explanation: I: 3(x + 1) + 4x = 2x(x + 1), so 2x² − 5x − 3 = 0 = (2x + 1)(x − 3), giving x = 3 or −0.5. II: (2y − 1)(2y − 3) = 0, so y = 0.5 or 1.5. x = 3 is above both y values, but x = −0.5 is below both. So the relationship cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y uses only x = 3; x ≤ y and x < y use only x = −0.5.
solution.final_answer: Option B: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The coefficients below are large. Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x² − 46x + 528 = 0
II. y² − 47y + 552 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Find two numbers with the given sum and product; near-equal roots must be compared pair by pair
solution.explanation: I: 22 + 24 = 46 and 22 × 24 = 528, so x = 22 or 24. II: 23 + 24 = 47 and 23 × 24 = 552, so y = 23 or 24. x = 22 is below both y values, but x = 24 is above y = 23. So the relationship cannot be established.
solution.shortcut: Half the sum gives the middle: 46/2 = 23 ⇒ roots 23 ± 1; 47/2 = 23.5 ⇒ roots 23.5 ± 0.5.
solution.why_others_wrong: x ≥ y and x > y use only x = 24; x < y uses only x = 22 and misses the pair x = 24, y = 23.
solution.final_answer: Option B: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the unit digit of 1234⁵⁶⁷ + 5678¹²³?

solution.concept: Only the unit digits matter: powers of 4 end in 4, 6, 4, 6, … and powers of 8 cycle 8, 4, 2, 6
solution.explanation: 1234⁵⁶⁷ ends like 4⁵⁶⁷; an odd power of 4 ends in 4. 5678¹²³ ends like 8¹²³; 123 = 4 × 30 + 3, so it ends like 8³ = 512, i.e. in 2. The sum ends in 4 + 2 = 6.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 multiplies the unit digits (4 × 2) instead of adding them; 0 takes 4⁵⁶⁷ as ending in 6 (an even power); 2 is the unit digit of the second term alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The HCF of two numbers is 27 and their LCM is 2,079. If one of the numbers lies between 250 and 300, what is the other number?

solution.concept: Write the numbers as 27a and 27b with a, b co-prime; then 27ab = LCM
solution.explanation: 2,079 ÷ 27 = 77 = 7 × 11, so (a, b) = (1, 77) or (7, 11). The pairs are 27 and 2,079, or 189 and 297. Only the second pair has a number between 250 and 300 (297), so the other number is 189.
solution.why_others_wrong: 297 is the number in the given range, not the other one; 77 is LCM ÷ HCF; 231 divides 2,079 by 9 instead of using the HCF 27.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many even factors does 720 have?

solution.concept: 720 = 2⁴ × 3² × 5; an even factor must contain at least one 2
solution.explanation: 720 = 2⁴ × 3² × 5. All factors: (4 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 30. Odd factors use 2⁰ only: (2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 6. Even factors = 30 − 6 = 24 (equivalently, choose 2¹ to 2⁴: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24).
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 counts all the factors; 6 counts only the odd factors; 20 uses 2⁴ × 3 × 5 and misses the 3².

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the smallest positive number that leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 5, a remainder of 3 when divided by 7 and a remainder of 4 when divided by 9?

solution.concept: Satisfy the conditions one at a time: list numbers fitting two of them (they repeat every LCM), then test the third
solution.explanation: Numbers leaving 4 on division by 9: 4, 13, 22, 31, … The first that also leaves 3 on division by 7 is 31; such numbers repeat every 63: 31, 94, 157, … Testing division by 5: 31 → 1, 94 → 4, 157 → 2 ✓. So the number is 157.
solution.why_others_wrong: 31 and 94 satisfy the conditions for 7 and 9 but not for 5; 472 also works but is the next such number (157 + 315), not the smallest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A's salary is 25% more than B's, and B's salary is 20% less than C's. A's salary is what percentage of C's?

solution.concept: Chain the multipliers: A = 1.25 B and B = 0.80 C
solution.explanation: B = 0.8 C, so A = 1.25 × 0.8 C = C. A's salary is 100% of C's.
solution.why_others_wrong: 105% adds the two percentages (+25 − 20 = +5); 95% subtracts them the other way; 125% compares A with B instead of with C.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A number is increased by 30% and the result is then decreased by 30%. The final value is 819. What was the original number?

solution.concept: Successive changes multiply: × 1.3 then × 0.7 = × 0.91
solution.explanation: The net multiplier is 1.3 × 0.7 = 0.91, so the original number = 819 ÷ 0.91 = 900.
solution.why_others_wrong: 819 assumes +30% and −30% cancel; 1,170 undoes only the 30% fall (819 ÷ 0.7); 745.29 applies the two changes to 819 again instead of reversing them.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a class, 40% of the students are girls. 25% of the boys and 35% of the girls scored a distinction. What percentage of the whole class scored a distinction?

solution.concept: The overall rate is a weighted average of the two rates, weighted by the share of boys and girls
solution.explanation: Take 100 students: 60 boys and 40 girls. Distinctions: 25% of 60 = 15 and 35% of 40 = 14, so 29 out of 100 = 29%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30% is the simple average of 25% and 35%; 31% swaps the weights (40% boys, 60% girls); 60% adds the two rates.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The radius of a cylinder is increased by 20% and its height is decreased by 20%. What is the percentage change in its volume?

solution.concept: Volume ∝ r²h, so the radius change enters twice: multiply 1.2 × 1.2 × 0.8
solution.explanation: New volume ÷ old volume = 1.2² × 0.8 = 1.44 × 0.8 = 1.152. The volume rises by 15.2%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'No change' assumes +20% and −20% cancel; '4% decrease' treats volume as r × h (1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96); '44% increase' squares the radius change but forgets the height.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a test, a candidate who scored 30% of the maximum marks failed by 15 marks, while another who scored 40% got 35 marks more than the pass mark. What percentage of the maximum marks is needed to pass?

solution.concept: Both statements describe the same pass mark: set 30% of M + 15 equal to 40% of M − 35
solution.why_others_wrong: 35% takes the mid-point of 30% and 40%; 37% subtracts 15 from the 40% score (200 − 15 = 185) instead of 35; 30% is the failing candidate's own score.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A car loses 15% of its value every year (on its value at the start of that year). After how many complete years will its value first fall below half of the purchase price?

solution.concept: Depreciation compounds: value after n years = P × 0.85ⁿ; find the first n with 0.85ⁿ < 0.5
solution.explanation: 0.85² = 0.7225, 0.85³ ≈ 0.614, 0.85⁴ ≈ 0.522 (still above half) and 0.85⁵ ≈ 0.444 (below half). So it first falls below half after 5 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 years stops too early (52.2% of the price is left); 3 years uses straight-line loss (50 ÷ 15 ≈ 3.3, rounded down); 6 years is one year after it has already fallen below half.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A family spends 40% of its income on food, 15% on rent and 25% on other items, and saves the rest. Its income rises by 10%, food costs rise by 25%, rent rises by 20% and other spending does not change. By what percentage do its savings change?

solution.concept: Take income = 100; update each spending head separately and recompute savings
solution.explanation: Old: spending 40 + 15 + 25 = 80, savings 20. New: income 110; food 50, rent 18, others 25, total 93; savings 17. Savings fall from 20 to 17, i.e. by 15%.
solution.why_others_wrong: '10% increase' assumes savings move with income; '3% decrease' gives the fall in rupees per 100 of old income, not as a percentage of the old savings; '15% increase' gets the sign of the change wrong.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Town P has 75,000 people and its population grows by 4% a year. Town Q has 90,000 people and its population falls by 5% a year. Both rates are applied on the population at the start of each year. After 2 years, which town has more people, and by how many?

solution.concept: Apply each rate twice (compounding) and compare
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Same population' applies the rates as simple (non-compounding) changes: 75,000 × 1.08 = 90,000 × 0.90 = 81,000; 'Town P, by 105' reverses the difference; 'Town Q, by 225' compounds Q's fall but treats P's growth as simple (81,000).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the fourth proportional to 12, 18 and 30?

solution.concept: x is the fourth proportional to a, b, c when a : b = c : x, so x = bc ÷ a
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 sets up 18 : 12 = 30 : x (the ratio reversed); 36 adds the difference 18 − 12 to 30 instead of keeping the ratio; 540 forgets to divide by 12.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A purse contains 50-paise, ₹1 and ₹2 coins worth ₹185 in all. There are twice as many ₹1 coins as 50-paise coins, and 5 fewer ₹2 coins than ₹1 coins. How many ₹2 coins are there?

solution.concept: Let the number of 50-paise coins be n and write the total value in rupees
solution.explanation: 50-paise coins: n; ₹1 coins: 2n; ₹2 coins: 2n − 5. Value: 0.5n + 2n + 2(2n − 5) = 6.5n − 10 = 185, so n = 30. ₹2 coins = 2 × 30 − 5 = 55.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 is the number of 50-paise coins; 60 is the number of ₹1 coins; 50 subtracts 10 instead of 5 from 60.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If (a + b) : (b + c) : (c + a) = 6 : 7 : 8 and a + b + c = 14, what is the value of c?

solution.concept: Adding the three sums gives 2(a + b + c); this fixes the scale k of the ratio
steps: Sum of the three = 2(a + b + c) = 28
solution.why_others_wrong: 14/3 is the value of a and 10/3 the value of b; 8 is a + b, not c.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum of money is divided among P, Q and R. P gets ₹300 more than two-fifths of the sum, Q gets ₹500 less than one-third of the sum, and R gets ₹2,600. What is the total sum?

solution.concept: Write each share in terms of the total S and use P + Q + R = S
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,900 is P's share; ₹9,750 forgets the ₹300 and ₹500 adjustments (4S/15 = 2,600); ₹10,500 moves the adjustments across with the wrong signs (4S/15 = 2,800).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average present age of a husband, his wife and their child is 27 years. Three years ago, the average age of the wife and the child was 20 years. What is the husband's present age?

solution.concept: Convert averages to totals, and move the past total to the present by adding 3 years for each person
solution.explanation: Present total of all three = 3 × 27 = 81. Three years ago, wife + child = 2 × 20 = 40, so now they total 40 + 6 = 46. Husband = 81 − 46 = 35 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 41 forgets to add 3 years to each of the wife and child; 38 adds 3 years only once; 47 subtracts 6 years instead of adding them.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A father is as many years old as his son is months old. The sum of their ages is 65 years. How old is the father?

solution.concept: The son's age in months is 12 times his age in years, so the father is 12 times as old as the son
solution.explanation: If the son is s years old, he is 12s months old, so the father is 12s years old. 12s + s = 65 gives s = 5, and the father is 60.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 years is the son's age; 55 takes the son as 10; 52 splits 65 in the ratio 4 : 1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: When Ravi was born, his father was 28 years old. Now the father is 1.8 times as old as Ravi. After how many years will the father be 1.5 times as old as Ravi?

solution.concept: The age gap (28 years) never changes; use it to find the present ages, then set up the future ratio
solution.explanation: Father − Ravi = 28 and Father = 1.8 × Ravi, so 0.8 × Ravi = 28: Ravi is 35 and the father 63. Then 63 + n = 1.5(35 + n) gives 0.5n = 10.5 and n = 21.
solution.shortcut: When F = 1.5R, the gap 28 = 0.5R, so R = 56: that is 56 − 35 = 21 years from now.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10.5 forgets to divide by 0.5; 28 is the age gap; 35 is Ravi's present age.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A family has a father, a mother and two children. The four ages now add up to 104 years. The father is 5 years older than the mother, and the elder child is 3 years older than the younger. When the younger child was born, the ages of the other three members added up to 64 years. What is the mother's present age?

solution.concept: Going back y years (the younger child's age) takes y years off each of the other three members
solution.explanation: Let the younger child be y. Then the other three now total 104 − y, and y years ago they totalled 104 − y − 3y = 104 − 4y = 64, so y = 10. The elder child is 13, so the parents total 104 − 23 = 81. With the father 5 years older, the mother is (81 − 5) ÷ 2 = 38.
solution.why_others_wrong: 43 is the father's age; 40.5 splits 81 equally and ignores the 5-year gap; 28 is the mother's age when the younger child was born.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average weight of A, B and C is 60 kg. The average weight of A and B is 56 kg, and that of B and C is 61 kg. What is B's weight?

solution.concept: Convert each average to a total; B is counted in both pair totals
solution.explanation: A + B + C = 180, A + B = 112 and B + C = 122. Adding the pair totals counts B twice: 112 + 122 = 234 = 180 + B, so B = 54 kg.
solution.why_others_wrong: 58 kg is A's weight; 68 kg is C's weight; 56 kg is the average of A and B, not B's own weight.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shop sold 120 items at an average price of ₹45 on Monday and 80 items at an average price of ₹60 on Tuesday. What was the average price of all the items sold on the two days?

solution.concept: Average of all items = total takings ÷ total items
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹52.50 is the simple average of 45 and 60, which ignores the numbers sold; ₹54 swaps the weights; ₹10,200 is the total takings, not the average.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average monthly salary of 15 workers is ₹18,000. A worker earning ₹24,000 leaves, and two new workers with equal salaries join. The average salary of the group is now ₹17,500. What is the salary of each new worker?

solution.concept: Track the total: remove the leaving worker's salary, then compare with the new total for the new group size
solution.explanation: Old total = 15 × 18,000 = ₹2,70,000. After the worker leaves: ₹2,46,000 for 14 workers. With two more there are 17 workers and the total is 17 × 17,500 = ₹2,97,500. The two new salaries add up to 2,97,500 − 2,46,000 = ₹51,500, so each is ₹25,750.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹51,500 is the two new salaries together; ₹17,000 counts the new group as 16 workers; ₹13,750 forgets to remove the leaving worker's ₹24,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of seven consecutive multiples of 3 is 45. What is the product of the smallest and the largest of them?

solution.concept: Consecutive multiples of 3 are equally spaced, so their average is the middle (4th) term
solution.explanation: The middle term is 45, so the numbers are 36, 39, 42, 45, 48, 51 and 54. The product of the smallest and largest is 36 × 54 = 1,944.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,025 = 45², the middle term squared; 1,989 = 39 × 51, the second and sixth terms; 2,016 = 42 × 48, the third and fifth terms.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a class, the 30 boys have an average height of 150 cm and the girls an average height of 140 cm; the average height of the whole class is 146 cm. Five boys with an average height of 152 cm leave the class, and five new girls with an average height of 138 cm join it. What is the new average height of the class?

solution.concept: First find the number of girls from the weighted average, then update the total height
solution.explanation: 30 × 150 + 140g = 146(30 + g) gives 4,500 + 140g = 4,380 + 146g, so g = 20 and the class has 50 students. Total height = 7,300 cm. Remove 5 × 152 = 760 and add 5 × 138 = 690: new total 7,230 cm for 50 students, so the new average is 144.6 cm.
solution.why_others_wrong: 145 cm assumes the leaving boys and joining girls are at their groups' averages (150 and 140); 146 cm assumes the average does not change because the class size is the same; 147.4 cm swaps the 760 and the 690.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A trader buys 25 kg of tea for ₹6,000 and sells all of it at ₹270 per kg. What is his profit percentage?

solution.concept: Profit % = (SP − CP) ÷ CP × 100, with both prices for the same quantity
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.11% divides the profit by the selling price (30 ÷ 270); 30% takes the ₹30 profit per kg as a percentage; 112.5% is SP as a percentage of CP.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper sells rice at its cost price but uses a false weight of 960 g in place of 1 kg. What is his gain percentage?

solution.concept: Gain % = error ÷ (true value given) × 100
solution.explanation: For every 960 g he gives, he charges the cost of 1,000 g. Gain = 40 g on 960 g = 40 ÷ 960 × 100 = 4⅙%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4% divides the 40 g by 1,000 g instead of by the 960 g actually given; 40% misplaces the decimal; 3.85% divides by 1,040 g.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sells an article to B at a profit of 10%, B sells it to C at a profit of 15%, and C sells it to D at a loss of 10%. If D pays ₹22,770, at what price did A buy it?

solution.concept: Successive selling prices multiply the cost by 1.10, 1.15 and 0.90
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹19,800 adds the rates (+10 + 15 − 10 = +15%); ₹18,000 ignores C's loss (22,770 ÷ 1.265); ₹20,700 undoes only A's 10% profit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An article is marked at ₹4,800. After a discount of 25%, the shopkeeper still makes a profit of 20%. What is its cost price?

solution.concept: SP = MP × (1 − discount) and SP = CP × (1 + profit)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,880 takes 20% off the SP instead of dividing by 1.2; ₹3,840 takes 20% off the marked price; ₹3,600 is the selling price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sells a mixer to B at a profit of 20%. B marks it 25% above his cost and sells it to C at a discount of 12%. C pays ₹480 more than A's cost. What was A's cost?

solution.concept: Chain the factors: C pays A's cost × 1.20 × 1.25 × 0.88
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,400 uses only A's 20% profit (480 ÷ 0.2); ₹1,920 uses only B's 25% mark-up; ₹1,980 is what C pays, not A's cost.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: After a discount of 15%, a cooler is sold for ₹3,230. How much is the discount in rupees?

solution.concept: SP = MP × 0.85, so MP = SP ÷ 0.85; discount = MP − SP
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹484.50 takes 15% of the selling price instead of the marked price; ₹3,800 is the marked price; ₹3,714.50 adds 15% to the selling price to get a marked price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An article marked at ₹6,000 is sold for ₹4,320 after two successive discounts. The first discount is twice the second. What is the first discount?

solution.concept: Successive discounts multiply: (1 − 2d)(1 − d) = 4,320 ÷ 6,000 = 0.72
solution.explanation: (1 − 2d)(1 − d) = 0.72 ⇒ 2d² − 3d + 0.28 = 0 ⇒ d = 0.1 (the other root, 1.4, is impossible). So the discounts are 20% and 10%: 6,000 × 0.8 × 0.9 = 4,320 ✓.
solution.shortcut: Try the options: 20% then 10% gives 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72 at once.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18⅔% splits the overall 28% in the ratio 2 : 1, as if successive discounts added; 28% is the single equivalent discount; 10% is the second discount.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A manufacturer marks his goods 50% above cost and sells them to a wholesaler at a discount of 20% on the marked price. The wholesaler sells them at the same marked price after two successive discounts of 10% and 5%. What is the wholesaler's profit percentage?

solution.concept: Work with the manufacturer's cost = 100; the wholesaler's cost is the manufacturer's selling price
solution.explanation: Marked price = 150. The wholesaler pays 150 × 0.8 = 120 and sells at 150 × 0.9 × 0.95 = 128.25. Profit = 8.25 on 120 = 6.875%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.25% divides the profit by the manufacturer's cost (100) instead of the wholesaler's (120); 6.25% adds the discounts to a single 15%; 28.25% measures the final price against the manufacturer's cost.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What sum of money earns a simple interest of ₹2,268 in 3 years at 7% per annum?

solution.why_others_wrong: ₹32,400 forgets the 3 years; ₹15,876 multiplies 2,268 by 7 instead of dividing; ₹13,068 is the amount (principal + interest), not the sum lent.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bank cut the simple interest rate on a deposit from 9% to 7.5% per annum. As a result, the depositor's yearly interest fell by ₹540. How much is the deposit?

solution.concept: The fall in yearly interest is the deposit × the fall in the rate
solution.explanation: The rate fell by 9 − 7.5 = 1.5 percentage points, so 1.5% of the deposit = ₹540 and the deposit = 540 ÷ 0.015 = ₹36,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹7,200 divides 540 by the new rate 7.5%; ₹6,000 divides by the old rate 9%; ₹3,600 misplaces a zero.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Arjun invested a sum at 10% per annum simple interest. After 2 years he withdrew the whole amount and invested it at 12% per annum simple interest for 3 more years, receiving ₹16,320 at the end. What sum did he invest at the start?

solution.concept: The amount after the first 2 years becomes the principal for the next 3 years
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹10,461.54 earns the 12% only on the original sum (1.56P); ₹12,000 is the amount after the first stage; ₹13,600 undoes only the first stage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the compound interest on ₹40,000 for 2 years at 7.5% per annum, compounded annually?

solution.concept: CI = P[(1 + r)ⁿ − 1]; for 2 years, CI = SI + interest on the first year's interest
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹6,000 is the simple interest; ₹46,225 is the amount, not the interest; ₹3,000 is one year's interest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What amount will ₹50,000 grow to in 1 year at 8% per annum compound interest, compounded half-yearly?

solution.concept: Half-yearly: halve the rate (4%) and double the number of periods (2)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹54,000 compounds annually (one period at 8%); ₹58,320 uses 8% per half-year; ₹4,080 is the interest, not the amount.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the difference between the compound interest (compounded annually) and the simple interest on ₹12,000 for 2 years at 15% per annum?

solution.concept: For 2 years, CI − SI = P × (r/100)²
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,800 is one year's interest; ₹135 halves the correct difference; ₹3,870 is the compound interest itself.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Meena deposits ₹10,000 at the start of each of two consecutive years in a scheme paying 10% per annum compound interest, compounded annually. What is the total in her account at the end of the second year?

solution.concept: Each deposit grows for the number of years it stays in the account
solution.explanation: The first ₹10,000 stays 2 years: 10,000 × 1.1² = ₹12,100. The second stays 1 year: 10,000 × 1.1 = ₹11,000. Total = ₹23,100.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹23,000 uses simple interest on the first deposit (12,000); ₹24,200 grows both deposits for 2 years; ₹22,000 grows both deposits for only 1 year.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi borrows ₹21,000 at 10% per annum compound interest, compounded annually. He repays ₹11,000 at the end of the first year. How much must he pay at the end of the second year to clear the loan?

solution.concept: Interest is charged each year on the balance outstanding at the start of that year
solution.explanation: End of year 1: 21,000 × 1.1 = ₹23,100; after paying ₹11,000 the balance is ₹12,100. End of year 2: 12,100 × 1.1 = ₹13,310.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹12,100 forgets the second year's interest; ₹14,410 grows the whole loan for 2 years but gives no interest credit for the ₹11,000 paid early; ₹14,200 uses simple interest on ₹21,000 for 2 years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum is invested at compound interest, compounded annually. The amounts after 3 years and after 5 years are in the ratio 25 : 36. What is the rate of interest per annum?

solution.concept: Between year 3 and year 5 the amount is multiplied by (1 + r)², whatever the principal
solution.why_others_wrong: 44% is the growth over the two years, not per year; 22% halves the 44% as if it were simple interest; 11% takes the difference 36 − 25 as the rate.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Deposit X pays 12% per annum compounded quarterly; deposit Y pays 12.5% per annum compounded annually. On ₹1,00,000 for one year, which deposit earns more interest, and by how much (to the nearest paisa)?

solution.concept: Compare effective annual rates: quarterly 12% means 3% per quarter for 4 quarters
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Y earns ₹500 more' compares 12% and 12.5% and ignores quarterly compounding; 'Y earns ₹50.88 more' gets the direction wrong; 'the same' assumes 12% quarterly equals 12.5% annually.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On a certain sum, the simple interest for 2 years is ₹3,000 and the compound interest (compounded annually) for 2 years at the same rate is ₹3,150. What is the compound interest on the same sum for 3 years at that rate?

solution.concept: CI − SI for 2 years is the interest on one year's interest: it gives the rate, and then the sum
solution.shortcut: Third-year interest = 10% of the amount after 2 years (18,150) = 1,815; 3,150 + 1,815 = 4,965.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹4,500 is the simple interest for 3 years; ₹4,725 scales the 2-year CI by 3/2; ₹4,650 adds a third year's interest on the principal only (₹1,500).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C invest ₹25,000, ₹35,000 and ₹40,000 in a business for the same period. A's share of the profit is ₹6,000. What is the total profit?

solution.concept: Shares are in the ratio of capitals, 25 : 35 : 40 = 5 : 7 : 8
solution.explanation: A's share is 25/100 of the profit, so the total profit = 6,000 × 100 ÷ 25 = ₹24,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹18,000 assumes equal shares (3 × 6,000); ₹15,000 uses C's capital in place of A's; ₹8,400 is B's share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A invests ₹30,000 in a business for a whole year. B invests ₹20,000 for the first 6 months and raises it to ₹35,000 for the next 6 months. Out of a year's profit of ₹46,000, what is A's share?

solution.concept: Profit shares are in the ratio of capital × time, adding B's two periods
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹22,000 is B's share; ₹27,600 uses only the starting capitals 30 : 20; ₹23,000 splits the profit equally.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B are partners, and A's capital is three-fourths of B's. A manages the business and draws a salary of ₹2,000 a month out of the profit; the rest of the profit is shared in the ratio of capitals. At the end of the year A and B receive equal amounts in all. What was the year's profit?

solution.concept: A's salary must make up exactly the gap between B's and A's capital shares
solution.explanation: Salary for the year = ₹24,000. The remainder R is shared 3 : 4, so B gets R/7 more than A. Equal totals mean R/7 = 24,000, so R = 1,68,000 and the profit = 1,68,000 + 24,000 = ₹1,92,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,68,000 is only the part shared in the capital ratio; ₹16,000 takes the salary as ₹2,000 for the whole year; ₹1,44,000 takes the gap between the shares as R/6 instead of R/7.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The capitals of A, B and C are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4 and their profits at the end of the business are in the ratio 4 : 3 : 2. If C's capital was invested for 3 months, for how many months was A's capital invested?

solution.concept: Profit ∝ capital × time, so time ∝ profit ÷ capital
solution.explanation: Times are in the ratio 4/2 : 3/3 : 2/4 = 2 : 1 : ½ = 4 : 2 : 1. C's 3 months is 1 part, so A's time is 4 × 3 = 12 months.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 months is B's period; ¾ month divides capital by profit instead of profit by capital; 3 months assumes everyone invested for the same time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B start a business with ₹40,000 and ₹50,000. At the end of every 4 months, A adds ₹10,000 to his capital while B withdraws ₹10,000 from his. Out of a profit of ₹1,08,000 at the end of the year, what is A's share?

solution.concept: Split the year into three 4-month periods and add capital × time for each partner
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹48,000 uses the starting capitals 4 : 5 (it is also B's correct share); ₹54,000 splits equally; ₹72,000 uses the final capitals 60,000 : 30,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a business, A gets one-third of the profit, B gets one-fourth and C gets the rest. A invested ₹40,000 for 12 months, B invested for 9 months and C invested for 6 months. How much did C invest?

solution.concept: Profit shares are proportional to capital × months; A's share fixes the value of one share
solution.explanation: A's capital × time = 40,000 × 12 = 4,80,000, which is 1/3 of the total, so the total is 14,40,000. C's share is 1 − 1/3 − 1/4 = 5/12, i.e. 6,00,000. Over 6 months, C's capital = 6,00,000 ÷ 6 = ₹1,00,000.
solution.shortcut: B's capital works out to 3,60,000 ÷ 9 = ₹40,000 by the same method.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹50,000 divides C's 6,00,000 by 12 months instead of 6; ₹40,000 is B's capital (and A's); ₹80,000 gives C one-third of the profit, like A.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In what ratio must 22-carat gold be mixed with 18-carat gold to get 20.5-carat gold?

solution.concept: Alligation: (mean − cheaper) : (dearer − mean) gives dearer : cheaper
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 : 5 reverses the alligation ratio; 1 : 1 would give 20 carat, not 20.5; 11 : 9 is just the ratio 22 : 18 of the purities.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A 30-litre mixture of milk and water contains 20% water. How much pure milk must be added so that water makes up only 12% of the mixture?

solution.concept: The quantity of water stays fixed; find the new total in which it is 12%
solution.explanation: Water = 20% of 30 = 6 litres. For 6 litres to be 12% of the mixture, the mixture must be 6 ÷ 0.12 = 50 litres. Milk to add = 50 − 30 = 20 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.4 litres takes 8% (20 − 12) of 30; 50 litres is the new total, not the milk added; 44 litres is all the milk in the final mixture.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A man covers 50 km in 4 hours, partly by cycle at 20 km/h and the rest on foot at 5 km/h. How many kilometres does he cover by cycle?

solution.concept: Alligation on speeds gives the ratio of the TIMES spent at each speed (average speed 12.5 km/h)
solution.explanation: Average speed = 50 ÷ 4 = 12.5 km/h. Time on cycle : time on foot = (12.5 − 5) : (20 − 12.5) = 1 : 1, i.e. 2 hours each. Distance by cycle = 20 × 2 = 40 km.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 km is the distance on foot; 25 km applies the 1 : 1 ratio to distances instead of times; 20 km assumes he cycled for only 1 hour.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many litres of pure alcohol must be added to 40 litres of a 15% alcohol solution to make it a 32% solution?

solution.concept: Alligation of 15% and 100%: (100 − 32) : (32 − 15) = solution : pure alcohol
solution.explanation: Solution : pure = 68 : 17 = 4 : 1, so pure alcohol = 40 ÷ 4 = 10 litres. Check: (6 + 10) ÷ 50 = 32% ✓.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.8 litres adds 17% of 40 and forgets that the volume grows; 12.8 litres is 32% of 40, the alcohol needed if the volume stayed 40; 160 litres reverses the alligation ratio.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A tank holds 100 litres of a 30% sugar syrup. Twenty litres are drawn off and replaced with a 50% sugar syrup, and then this is done once more. What is the sugar concentration of the final syrup?

solution.concept: Each operation keeps 80% of the existing syrup and adds 20 litres at 50%
solution.explanation: After the first operation: 80 litres at 30% (24 L sugar) + 20 litres at 50% (10 L) = 34 L sugar, i.e. 34%. After the second: 80 litres at 34% (27.2 L) + 10 L = 37.2 L sugar in 100 litres = 37.2%.
solution.shortcut: The gap to 50% shrinks by 20% each time: 20 → 16 → 12.8, so 50 − 12.8 = 37.2%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 34% stops after one operation; 38% assumes each operation adds the same 4 points; 40% simply averages 30% and 50%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 6 painters can paint 3 identical houses in 8 days. In how many days can 4 painters paint 2 such houses?

solution.concept: Work = painters × days; one house needs a fixed number of painter-days
solution.explanation: 3 houses need 6 × 8 = 48 painter-days, so one house needs 16. Two houses need 32 painter-days; with 4 painters that is 32 ÷ 4 = 8 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 days ignores the drop from 3 houses to 2; 5⅓ days ignores the drop from 6 painters to 4; 18 days applies the house ratio upside down (8 × 6/4 × 3/2).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A can finish a job in 12 days and B in 18 days. A works alone for the first 3 days, and then A and B together finish the job. The payment of ₹3,600 is shared in proportion to the work each did. What is B's share?

solution.concept: Find how long B worked, then B's share of the work = days worked ÷ B's time for the whole job
solution.explanation: A does 3/12 = 1/4 alone. The remaining 3/4 at the joint rate 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 per day takes 27/5 = 5.4 days. B worked 5.4 days, i.e. 5.4/18 = 0.3 of the job, so B gets 0.3 × 3,600 = ₹1,080.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,440 splits the money in the ratio of efficiencies 3 : 2, ignoring A's 3 days alone; ₹1,800 splits it equally; ₹2,520 is A's share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C can finish a job alone in 8, 12 and 16 days respectively. They work one at a time in turn: A on the 1st day, B on the 2nd, C on the 3rd, A on the 4th, and so on. On which day is the job completed?

solution.concept: Take the work as 48 units: A does 6, B 4 and C 3 units a day, i.e. 13 units per 3-day cycle
solution.explanation: Three cycles (9 days) complete 39 units, leaving 9. Day 10 (A) does 6 → 45 units. Day 11 (B) needs only 3 of its 4 units, so the job is completed on the 11th day.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10th day leaves 3 units undone after A's turn; 12th day overshoots by a full day; 9th day leaves 9 units after three complete cycles.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 12 men can finish a job in 18 days, and 18 women can finish it in 20 days. 6 men start the job and work alone for 12 days; then 10 women join them. In how many days in all is the job finished?

solution.concept: Convert men and women to work units per day using a common total
solution.explanation: Take the job as 1,080 units: a man does 1,080 ÷ 216 = 5 units a day and a woman 1,080 ÷ 360 = 3. Six men in 12 days do 6 × 5 × 12 = 360 units, leaving 720. With 10 women, the daily output is 30 + 30 = 60 units, so 720 units take 12 more days. Total = 12 + 12 = 24 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 days counts only the time after the women join; 21 days treats a woman as working as fast as a man (720 ÷ 80 = 9 more days); 36 days is the time for the 6 men working alone throughout.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B can finish a job alone in 20 and 30 days. They start together, but A leaves 5 days before the job is finished. The payment of ₹15,000 is shared in proportion to the work done. What is A's share?

solution.concept: If the job takes T days, B works T days and A works T − 5 days
solution.explanation: (T − 5)/20 + T/30 = 1 ⇒ 3(T − 5) + 2T = 60 ⇒ T = 15. A worked 10 days and did 10/20 = 1/2 of the job, so A's share = ₹7,500.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹9,000 splits by the efficiencies 3 : 2 as if both worked throughout; ₹6,000 splits by days worked 10 : 15; ₹10,000 gives A 10/15 of the money (his days as a share of the total time).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B work on a job on alternate days. If A works on the first day, the job is finished in exactly 17 days. If B works on the first day, it is finished in 17½ days. In how many days can A alone finish the job?

solution.concept: Count the working days of each person in both orders and compare
solution.explanation: A first: A works 9 days and B 8 days, so 9a + 8b = 1. B first: B works 9 days, A 8 days and A works half of the 18th day, so 9b + 8.5a = 1. Equating, 9a + 8b = 8.5a + 9b ⇒ 0.5a = b. Then 9a + 4a = 13a = 1, so A takes 13 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 26 days is B's time; 17 days assumes A and B are equally fast; 8⅔ days is the time for A and B working together.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 20 minutes and 30 minutes. Both are opened on the empty tank, and after 6 minutes pipe A is closed. How long does it take in all to fill the tank?

solution.concept: Work out the part filled while both run, then the time B alone needs for the rest
solution.explanation: Together they fill 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12 per minute, so in 6 minutes they fill 1/2. B fills the other half in ½ × 30 = 15 minutes. Total = 6 + 15 = 21 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 minutes is only B's time after A closes; 12 minutes is the time if both stay open; 16 minutes uses A's rate for the second half (6 + 10).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipes A and B can each fill a tank on their own, in 12 minutes and 16 minutes respectively. Pipe A delivers 3 litres per minute more than pipe B. What is the capacity of the tank?

solution.concept: Rate = capacity ÷ time; the difference of the two rates is 3 litres per minute
solution.explanation: C/12 − C/16 = C/48 = 3, so C = 144 litres. (A: 12 L/min, B: 9 L/min.)
steps: A's rate = C/12, B's rate = C/16
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 litres is 3 × 16; 36 litres is 3 × 12; 576 litres is 3 × 12 × 16 without dividing by the 4-minute gap between the two times.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A pipe can fill a tank in 3 hours. When the tank is half full, three more pipes of the same size are opened. How long does it take in all to fill the tank, starting from empty?

solution.concept: The first half takes half the single pipe's time; then four pipes work together
solution.explanation: One pipe fills half the tank in 1.5 hours. Then 4 pipes fill at 4/3 of the tank per hour, so the other half takes ½ ÷ 4/3 = 3/8 hour = 22½ minutes. Total = 1 h 30 min + 22½ min = 1 hour 52½ minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 hours counts only 3 pipes in all after the half-way point; 45 minutes assumes all four pipes run from the start; 3 hours ignores the extra pipes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 20 minutes and 30 minutes, and pipe C can empty the full tank in 15 minutes. Starting with the tank empty, the pipes are opened one at a time for one minute each in the order A, B, C, A, B, C, … . After how many minutes is the tank first full?

solution.concept: Net gain per 3-minute cycle is small, but the tank can fill during a B-minute before C empties it
solution.explanation: Take the tank as 60 units: A adds 3, B adds 2 and C removes 4 units, a net 1 unit per cycle. Within a cycle the level peaks after B at (start + 5). So the tank is full once start + 5 ≥ 60, i.e. after 55 complete cycles (165 minutes, level 55): A brings it to 58 and B to 60 at the 167th minute.
solution.why_others_wrong: 180 minutes divides 60 units by the net 1 unit per cycle and ignores the peak within a cycle; 172 minutes waits for an A-minute to finish the job; 168 minutes counts the whole 56th cycle.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A car covers 35 km in the first hour of a journey, and its speed rises by 2 km/h every hour after that. What is its average speed over the first 12 hours?

solution.concept: The hourly distances form an arithmetic progression; the average equals (first + last) ÷ 2
solution.explanation: The 12 hourly distances are 35, 37, …, 57 km. Total = 12 × (35 + 57) ÷ 2 = 552 km, so the average speed is 552 ÷ 12 = 46 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 57 km/h is the speed in the last hour; 35 km/h is the speed in the first hour; 47 km/h counts 12 increases instead of 11 (last speed 59).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two cyclists start from the same point at the same time and ride in opposite directions at 12 km/h and 18 km/h. After how long will they be 75 km apart?

solution.concept: Moving apart in opposite directions, the gap grows at the sum of the speeds
solution.explanation: The gap grows at 12 + 18 = 30 km/h, so 75 km takes 75 ÷ 30 = 2.5 hours = 2 hours 30 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 h 30 min uses the difference of speeds (6 km/h); 6 h 15 min uses only the slower speed; 4 h 10 min uses only the faster speed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: At 6:00 AM, P and Q start walking towards each other from two places 100 km apart, at 15 km/h and 25 km/h. They keep walking after they meet. At what time will they be 20 km apart for the second time?

solution.concept: They are 20 km apart once before meeting and once after crossing; the closing speed is 40 km/h throughout
solution.explanation: Before meeting, the gap is 20 km after covering 80 km together: 80 ÷ 40 = 2 h (8:00 AM). After crossing, they are 20 km apart when together they have covered 120 km: 120 ÷ 40 = 3 h, i.e. at 9:00 AM.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8:00 AM is the first time they are 20 km apart; 8:30 AM is when they meet; 10:00 AM uses only Q's speed (100 ÷ 25 = 4 h).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A man walking up a moving escalator reaches the top in 24 seconds. Standing still on the moving escalator, he reaches the top in 40 seconds. How long would he take to walk up the escalator if it were not moving?

solution.concept: Speeds add: walking speed + escalator speed = his speed on the moving escalator
solution.explanation: Per second he covers 1/24 of the escalator walking on it while it moves, and the escalator alone covers 1/40. His own walking covers 1/24 − 1/40 = 1/60 per second, so he would take 60 seconds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 seconds adds the two rates instead of subtracting; 32 seconds averages the two times; 16 seconds subtracts the times (40 − 24).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A car travels for the first 2 hours at 50 km/h and then covers the next 150 km at 75 km/h. At what speed must it cover the remaining 100 km so that its average speed for the whole 350 km is 50 km/h?

solution.concept: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time; find the time left for the last part
solution.explanation: The whole 350 km at 50 km/h must take 7 hours. The first part (100 km) took 2 hours and the second 150 ÷ 75 = 2 hours. So 100 km must be covered in 3 hours, at 100 ÷ 3 = 33⅓ km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 km/h averages the three speeds; 50 km/h assumes the last part must match the target average; 66⅔ km/h forgets that the first 2 hours covered 100 km (200 km left in 3 h).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Buses leave town X for town Y every 20 minutes and run at 40 km/h. A man rides a scooter from Y towards X at 20 km/h along the same road. How often does he meet a bus coming towards him?

solution.concept: Successive buses are a fixed distance apart; he closes that gap at the sum of the speeds
solution.explanation: Buses 20 minutes apart at 40 km/h are 40 × ⅓ = 13⅓ km apart. Moving towards them, the man closes the gap at 40 + 20 = 60 km/h, so he meets a bus every 13⅓ ÷ 60 hour = 13⅓ minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Every 20 minutes' ignores his own motion; 'every 40 minutes' uses the difference of speeds, as if he rode in the same direction as the buses; 'every 10 minutes' scales 20 minutes by the speed ratio 20 : 40.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A swimmer swims 2 km against the current in 40 minutes and swims back the same 2 km with the current in 24 minutes. What is her speed in still water?

solution.concept: Still-water speed = (downstream speed + upstream speed) ÷ 2
solution.explanation: Upstream: 2 km in 40 min = 3 km/h. Downstream: 2 km in 24 min = 5 km/h. Still-water speed = (5 + 3) ÷ 2 = 4 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 km/h is the speed of the current; 8 km/h adds the two speeds without halving; 3.75 km/h is her average speed for the round trip (4 km in 64 minutes).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat's speed in still water is three times the speed of the stream. It goes 24 km downstream in 3 hours. How long does the round trip (24 km downstream and back) take?

solution.concept: If the stream is s, the boat is 3s: downstream = 4s, upstream = 2s
solution.explanation: Downstream speed = 24 ÷ 3 = 8 km/h = 4s, so s = 2 km/h and the boat is 6 km/h. Upstream speed = 4 km/h, so the return takes 24 ÷ 4 = 6 hours. Round trip = 3 + 6 = 9 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 hours is only the return journey; 7 hours takes the upstream speed as the still-water speed 6 km/h; 12 hours doubles the upstream time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat with a speed of 12 km/h in still water makes a 35 km trip downstream and back. If the speed of the stream rises from 2 km/h to 3 km/h, how much longer does the round trip take?

solution.concept: Compute both round-trip times; the slower upstream leg loses more time than the faster downstream leg saves
solution.explanation: Stream 2 km/h: 35/14 + 35/10 = 2.5 + 3.5 = 6 hours. Stream 3 km/h: 35/15 + 35/9 = 2⅓ + 3 8/9 = 6 2/9 hours. The difference is 2/9 hour = 13⅓ minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'No longer' assumes the gain downstream cancels the loss upstream; 23⅓ minutes counts only the extra time upstream; 10 minutes counts only the time saved downstream.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train 200 m long crosses a bridge 400 m long in 30 seconds. What is the speed of the train in km/h?

solution.concept: To cross a bridge, the train covers its own length plus the bridge; 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 km/h uses only the bridge's length; 24 km/h uses only the train's length; 20 is the speed in m/s, not km/h.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train 120 m long running at 60 km/h overtakes a train 180 m long running in the same direction on a parallel track, and passes it completely in 36 seconds. What is the speed of the slower train?

solution.concept: Overtaking covers the sum of the lengths at the difference of the speeds
solution.explanation: Relative speed = (120 + 180) ÷ 36 = 25/3 m/s = 25/3 × 18/5 = 30 km/h. Slower train = 60 − 30 = 30 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 90 km/h adds the relative speed, as if the trains ran towards each other; 42 km/h uses only the 180 m train's length; 8⅓ is the relative speed in m/s.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train passes completely through a 300 m long platform in 30 seconds. It passes a man walking on the platform at 6 km/h towards the train (in the opposite direction) in 9 seconds. What is the length of the train?

solution.concept: Use L + 300 = 30v for the platform and L = 9 × (v + man's speed) for the man; 6 km/h = 5/3 m/s
solution.why_others_wrong: 128.57 m ignores the man's speed (L = 9v); 107.14 m takes him as walking in the same direction as the train; 450 m is the length of the train plus the platform.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The area of a circular plot is 616 m². What is its circumference? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Find r from πr² = area, then circumference = 2πr
solution.why_others_wrong: 44 m uses r = 7 (half the radius); 176 m uses r = 28 (the diameter as the radius); 196 is r², not the circumference.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The radii of two cylinders are in the ratio 2 : 3 and their heights are in the ratio 5 : 3. What is the ratio of their volumes?

solution.concept: Volume = πr²h, so the radius ratio is squared and the height ratio is not
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 : 9 forgets to square the radii; 4 : 9 ignores the heights; 27 : 20 inverts the ratio.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A rectangular lawn measures 50 m × 30 m. A path 2 m wide runs along all four sides inside the lawn. What is the area of the path?

solution.concept: Area of an inside path = outer area − inner area, where each inner side is shorter by 2 × width
solution.why_others_wrong: 320 m² multiplies the perimeter by the width and counts the four corner squares twice; 336 m² is a 2 m path outside the lawn; 1,196 m² is the area inside the path.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A path of uniform width runs around the outside of a rectangular garden 40 m long and 30 m wide. The area of the path is 456 m². What is the width of the path?

solution.concept: Outer rectangle = (40 + 2w)(30 + 2w); the path's area gives a quadratic in w
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.26 m divides 456 by the perimeter 140 and ignores the four corner squares; 6 m adds the width only once to each dimension, (40 + w)(30 + w); 3.63 m treats the path as lying inside the garden.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The largest possible sphere is carved out of a solid cube of edge 14 cm. What volume of the cube is cut away? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: The largest sphere in a cube has diameter equal to the edge, so r = 7 cm
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,437⅓ cm³ is the volume of the sphere; 2,744 cm³ is the whole cube; 1,372 cm³ uses π = 3 instead of the stated 22/7.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability of getting a doublet (both dice showing the same number) or a total of 4?

solution.concept: Count the outcomes in the union once each: (2, 2) is both a doublet and a total of 4
solution.explanation: Doublets: 6 outcomes. Total 4: (1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 1). (2, 2) is in both, so the union has 6 + 3 − 1 = 8 outcomes, and the probability is 8/36 = 2/9.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/4 counts (2, 2) twice (9/36); 1/6 counts only the doublets; 1/12 counts only the totals of 4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bag contains 25 balls numbered 1 to 25. One ball is drawn at random. What is the probability that its number is a prime?

solution.concept: List the primes up to 25; 1 is not prime and 2 is
solution.explanation: Primes from 1 to 25: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 — nine numbers. Probability = 9/25.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2/5 counts 1 as a prime (10/25); 8/25 leaves out 2, the only even prime; 16/25 is the probability of NOT getting a prime.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three cards are drawn together at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that all three are face cards (jack, queen or king)?

solution.concept: Use combinations for both counts: ¹²C₃ favourable out of ⁵²C₃
solution.explanation: There are 12 face cards. ¹²C₃ = 220 and ⁵²C₃ = 22,100, so the probability = 220/22,100 = 11/1105.
solution.why_others_wrong: 27/2197 = (12/52)³ assumes each card is replaced before the next draw; 3/13 is the probability for a single card; 66/1105 counts the favourable cards in order (12 × 11 × 10) but the total without order.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bag contains 5 white and 3 black balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other, the first being replaced before the second is drawn. What is the probability that the two balls are of different colours?

solution.concept: With replacement the draws are independent; 'different colours' can happen as WB or BW
solution.explanation: P(W then B) = 5/8 × 3/8 = 15/64 and P(B then W) = 15/64, so P(different) = 30/64 = 15/32.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15/64 counts only one order; 15/28 draws without replacement; 17/32 is the probability that the colours are the same.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two fair dice are rolled, and you are told that at least one of them shows a 6. What is the probability that the total is 10 or more?

solution.concept: Conditional probability: count only within the outcomes that have at least one 6
solution.explanation: Outcomes with at least one 6: 11. Of these, totals of 10 or more are (4, 6), (6, 4), (5, 6), (6, 5) and (6, 6) — 5 outcomes. Probability = 5/11.
steps: Reduced sample space: 11 outcomes with a 6
solution.why_others_wrong: 5/36 forgets the condition and divides by all 36 outcomes; 1/6 is the unconditional chance of a total of 10 or more (6/36); 6/11 also counts (5, 5), which has no 6.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many ways can 5 people sit in a row of 5 chairs if two particular people must sit next to each other?

solution.concept: Tie the two people together as one unit, arrange the units, then arrange the two inside the unit
solution.explanation: Treat the pair as one unit: 4 units can be arranged in 4! = 24 ways, and the pair can sit in 2 orders. Total = 24 × 2 = 48.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 forgets that the two can swap places; 120 ignores the condition; 72 counts the arrangements in which the two are NOT together.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many ways can the letters of the word CREDIT be arranged so that the two vowels are never next to each other?

solution.concept: Never together = all arrangements − arrangements with the vowels together
solution.explanation: All arrangements: 6! = 720. With E and I together: treat them as one unit, 5! × 2 = 240. Never together = 720 − 240 = 480.
solution.shortcut: Gap method: arrange C, R, D, T in 4! = 24 ways and place E, I in 2 of the 5 gaps: ⁵P₂ = 20; 24 × 20 = 480.
solution.why_others_wrong: 240 counts the arrangements with the vowels together; 600 forgets that E and I can swap within their unit (720 − 120); 720 ignores the condition.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many ways can 3 books be chosen from 8 different books if two particular books must never both be chosen?

solution.concept: Subtract the selections that contain both of the two books
solution.explanation: All selections: ⁸C₃ = 56. Selections containing both particular books: the third book can be any of the other 6, so 6. Allowed = 56 − 6 = 50.
solution.why_others_wrong: 56 ignores the condition; 20 leaves out both books altogether (⁶C₃); 44 subtracts the 6 bad selections twice.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A team of 4 is to be chosen from 6 batsmen and 4 bowlers so that it has at least one bowler, and then one of the 4 chosen players is to be made captain. In how many ways can this be done?

solution.concept: Count the teams with at least one bowler (complement), then multiply by the 4 choices of captain
solution.explanation: Teams of 4 from 10: ¹⁰C₄ = 210. Teams with no bowler: ⁶C₄ = 15. So 195 teams have at least one bowler. Each can choose its captain in 4 ways: 195 × 4 = 780.
solution.why_others_wrong: 195 forgets to choose the captain; 840 drops the 'at least one bowler' condition; 1,344 counts 'pick one bowler, then any 3 others' (4 × ⁹C₃), which counts teams with two or more bowlers several times.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many tonnes of made tea did Borjan produce in 2025?

solution.concept: Production = area × yield; convert kg to tonnes by dividing by 1,000
solution.explanation: Borjan: 320 ha × 2,500 kg/ha = 8,00,000 kg = 800 tonnes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 80 tonnes and 8,000 tonnes slip a zero in the conversion; 280 tonnes is Borjan's orthodox tea only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many tonnes of CTC tea did Chandra produce in 2025?

solution.concept: CTC share = 100% − orthodox share
solution.explanation: Chandra produced 500 × 1,800 = 9,00,000 kg = 900 tonnes, of which 10% (90 tonnes) was orthodox. CTC = 90% of 900 = 810 tonnes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 90 tonnes is the orthodox tea; 900 tonnes is the whole production; 720 tonnes uses Amguri's 20% orthodox share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which estate produced the largest quantity of orthodox tea in 2025?

solution.concept: Orthodox tea = area × yield × orthodox share; compare the products, not the percentages
solution.explanation: Orthodox tea (tonnes): Amguri 180, Borjan 280, Chandra 90, Dhelakhat 252, Erabari 270. Borjan is the largest.
solution.why_others_wrong: Erabari has the largest total production but only 270 tonnes of orthodox tea; Dhelakhat has the highest orthodox percentage but a small area (252 tonnes); Amguri produces only 180 tonnes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of the total production of the five estates was orthodox tea (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Overall share = total orthodox ÷ total production; the estates' percentages must be weighted by production
solution.why_others_wrong: 25.20% is the simple average of the five percentages; 23.15% weights the percentages by area instead of by production; 75.53% is the CTC share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Orthodox tea sells at ₹420 per kg and CTC tea at ₹240 per kg. What was Erabari's revenue from its 2025 production?

solution.concept: Split the production into orthodox and CTC, price each, then add
