solution.explanation: Erabari: 1,080 tonnes, 25% orthodox. Orthodox 270 t = 2,70,000 kg × ₹420 = ₹11.34 crore. CTC 810 t = 8,10,000 kg × ₹240 = ₹19.44 crore. Total = ₹30.78 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹25.92 crore prices all the tea as CTC; ₹45.36 crore prices it all as orthodox; ₹35.64 crore uses the simple average price ₹330.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Next year Chandra keeps the same area, its yield rises by 25% and its orthodox share doubles. By what percentage does its orthodox production increase?

solution.concept: Orthodox output = area × yield × share; multiply the change factors: 1.25 × 2
solution.explanation: New production = 900 × 1.25 = 1,125 tonnes; new orthodox share = 20%, so orthodox = 225 tonnes against 90 now. Increase = 135 ÷ 90 = 150%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 100% counts only the doubled share; 125% adds the two changes (25% + 100%) instead of multiplying the factors; 25% counts only the yield rise.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the total amount of the 1-year deposits booked in the quarter?

solution.concept: Total amount = number of deposits × average deposit
solution.explanation: 300 deposits × ₹2.5 lakh = ₹750 lakh = ₹7.5 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹75 crore slips a decimal place in converting lakh to crore; ₹9 crore is the 2-year (or 3-year) total; ₹2.5 crore confuses the average deposit in lakh with the total.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average size of a deposit across all four tenures taken together?

solution.concept: Overall average = total amount ÷ total number of deposits (a weighted average)
solution.explanation: Total amount = 750 + 900 + 900 + 950 = ₹3,500 lakh; total deposits = 300 + 200 + 150 + 50 = 700. Average = 3,500 ÷ 700 = ₹5 lakh.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹8 lakh is the simple average of the four averages; ₹4.375 lakh divides the total by 800 deposits (a miscount); ₹50 lakh slips a decimal place.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Interest on the 3-year deposits is compounded annually at the rate shown. What total interest will be payable on all the 3-year deposits at maturity (in ₹ lakh, correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Total 3-year amount = 150 × 6 = ₹900 lakh; CI = P(1.07³ − 1)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹189 lakh is simple interest for 3 years; ₹1,102.54 lakh is the maturity amount, not the interest; ₹63 lakh is one year's interest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the average interest rate on all the deposits booked, weighted by the amount deposited (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Weight each rate by the rupee amount of that tenure: Σ(amount × rate) ÷ Σ amount
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.89% is the simple average of the four rates; 6.75% weights the rates by the number of deposits, not the amount; 7.25% is just the highest rate.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Senior citizens hold 40% (by amount) of the 3-year deposits and receive 0.5% per annum more than the rate shown. What is the total simple interest for one year on all the 3-year deposits?

solution.concept: Interest at 7% on the whole amount, plus an extra 0.5% on the senior citizens' 40%
solution.explanation: Total 3-year amount = ₹900 lakh. At 7%: ₹63 lakh. Senior citizens' share = ₹360 lakh, extra 0.5% = ₹1.8 lakh. Total = ₹64.8 lakh.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹67.5 lakh pays 7.5% on everyone's deposits; ₹63 lakh ignores the senior-citizen extra; ₹65.7 lakh applies the extra to 60% of the deposits instead of 40%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In which year was the disbursement exactly 25% more than in the previous year?

solution.concept: Percentage change = (this year − previous year) ÷ previous year × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 2021-22 rose 20%; 2024-25 rose 40%; 2025-26 rose 33⅓% (315 ÷ 945), which is 25% only if the rise is divided by the later year's 1,260.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did the yearly disbursement grow from 2020-21 to 2025-26?

solution.concept: Overall growth compares the two end years directly; yearly growth rates cannot simply be added
solution.why_others_wrong: 108⅓% adds the five yearly rates (20 − 10 + 25 + 40 + 33⅓); 252% is 1,260 as a percentage of 500, not the increase; 60.32% divides the increase by the later year's 1,260.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In 2024-25 the bank disbursed 63,000 gold loans. In 2025-26 the average size of a gold loan was 20% higher than in 2024-25. How many gold loans did the bank disburse in 2025-26?

solution.concept: Number of loans = amount disbursed ÷ average loan size
solution.explanation: 2024-25 average = ₹945 crore ÷ 63,000 = ₹1.5 lakh. 2025-26 average = ₹1.8 lakh. Number in 2025-26 = ₹1,260 crore ÷ ₹1.8 lakh = 70,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: 84,000 keeps the 2024-25 average of ₹1.5 lakh; 63,000 assumes the number of loans did not change; 75,600 raises the number of loans by 20% instead of the loan size.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many of the five states did wind make up more than 40% of the new capacity added?

solution.concept: Wind share = wind ÷ (solar + wind) for each state; 'more than 40%' excludes exactly 40%
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 counts State A, whose share is exactly 40%; 2 misses State E (46%); 5 counts every state.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Each MW of solar capacity generates 1.6 million units (MU) of electricity a year and each MW of wind capacity 2.4 MU a year. Which state's new capacity will generate the most electricity in a year?

solution.concept: Generation = solar MW × 1.6 + wind MW × 2.4; the state with the most MW need not generate the most
solution.why_others_wrong: State E adds the most capacity (2,500 MW) but much of it is solar (4,920 MU); State C adds the most solar but generates only 3,720 MU; State D has the highest wind share but a small total (3,840 MU).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Solar capacity costs ₹4.2 crore per MW to set up and wind capacity ₹6.5 crore per MW. The investment in State E's new capacity is what percentage more than that in State A's (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Price the solar and wind parts separately for each state, then compare the totals
solution.why_others_wrong: 25.00% compares the capacities (2,500 vs 2,000 MW) and ignores the different costs; 22.10% divides the difference by E's investment instead of A's; 43.75% compares only the wind parts (1,150 vs 800 MW).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many out-patients visited the Orthopaedics department?

solution.concept: Number = (central angle ÷ 360) × total
solution.explanation: Orthopaedics: 45/360 × 7,200 = 900 patients.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,080 is the Paediatrics figure; 450 and 4,500 multiply the angle by 10 or 100 instead of scaling by 7,200/360 = 20.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of the out-patients visited the Gynaecology department?

solution.concept: Percentage = angle ÷ 360 × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 63% reads the angle as a percentage; 21% divides by 300 instead of 360; 12.6% divides by 500.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The number of Dermatology patients is what percentage less than the number of Paediatrics patients?

solution.concept: Percentage less = difference ÷ the larger (base) value × 100; angles can be compared directly
solution.explanation: Dermatology 36° (720 patients), Paediatrics 54° (1,080). Difference = 18° on 54° = 1/3 = 33⅓% less.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50% divides the difference by Dermatology's angle; 18% takes the 18° gap as a percentage; 66⅔% is Dermatology as a percentage of Paediatrics.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The consultation fee is ₹300 in General Medicine and ₹500 in every other department. A quarter of the General Medicine patients were senior citizens, who paid half the fee. What was the total fee collected in October?

solution.concept: Find the General Medicine patients, split them into full-fee and half-fee, and price the other departments at ₹500
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹31,68,000 ignores the senior citizens' half fee; ₹36,00,000 charges every patient ₹500; ₹25,20,000 leaves out General Medicine altogether.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the amount of housing loans outstanding in March 2026?

solution.concept: Use each year's own total with that year's percentage
solution.explanation: March 2026: 28% of ₹3,000 crore = ₹840 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹672 crore applies 2026's 28% to 2025's total; ₹750 crore applies 2025's 25% to 2026's total; ₹600 crore is the March 2025 figure.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which sector's loans grew the most, in percentage terms, from March 2025 to March 2026?

solution.concept: Convert both years' percentages to rupees before comparing growth; shares of different totals cannot be compared directly
solution.explanation: Amounts (₹ crore) 2025 → 2026: Agriculture 432 → 480 (+11.1%), MSME 528 → 720 (+36.4%), Housing 600 → 840 (+40%), Personal 360 → 420 (+16.7%), Corporate 480 → 540 (+12.5%). Housing grew the most.
solution.why_others_wrong: MSME grew 36.4%, second to housing; Personal grew only 16.7% even though its amount rose; Agriculture's share fell and its amount rose just 11.1%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By how much did the loans outstanding in all sectors other than housing increase from March 2025 to March 2026?

solution.concept: Non-housing loans = total − housing, for each year
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹600 crore is the increase in the whole loan book; ₹240 crore is the increase in housing loans alone; ₹180 crore applies the 2025 non-housing share (75%) to the 2026 total (2,250 − 1,800).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much cargo did the port handle in the second quarter (April to June)?

solution.concept: Add the three monthly points of the quarter
solution.explanation: April 1,071 + May 918 + June 1,224 = 3,213 thousand tonnes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,583 is the first quarter's total; 2,907 adds March to May; 1,224 is June alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In which month was the percentage fall in cargo, compared with the previous month, the largest?

solution.concept: Percentage fall = fall ÷ previous month's value; the biggest drop in tonnes need not be the biggest in percent
solution.explanation: Falls: February 900 → 765, a fall of 135 on 900 = 15%; May 1,071 → 918, a fall of 153 on 1,071 ≈ 14.3%. The other months rose. The largest percentage fall is in February.
solution.why_others_wrong: May has the larger fall in tonnes (153) but the smaller fall in percent; June and April were months of rising cargo.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average monthly cargo handled over the six months?

solution.concept: Average = sum of the six values ÷ 6
solution.why_others_wrong: 861 is the first quarter's average; 1,071 is the second quarter's average; 1,062 averages only January and June.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of the six months' cargo was handled in the second quarter (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Share = quarter total ÷ six-month total × 100
solution.explanation: Second quarter = 3,213; six-month total = 5,796. Share = 3,213 ÷ 5,796 = 55.43%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 44.57% is the first quarter's share; 124.39% compares the second quarter with the first; 50.00% assumes the two quarters were equal.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Containers made up 40% of the cargo in the first quarter and 45% in the second quarter. By what percentage did the container cargo increase from the first quarter to the second (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Container cargo = share × quarter total; then compare the two quarters
solution.why_others_wrong: 12.50% compares only the shares (45 ÷ 40); 24.39% is the growth of all cargo; 5.00% is the rise in the share in percentage points.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many savings accounts did Bank Q have at the end of 2023?

solution.concept: Apply each year's growth rate in turn to the previous year's number
solution.why_others_wrong: 58 lakh adds the two rates (45%) instead of compounding them; 48 lakh applies only the 2023 rate to the 2021 figure; 66 lakh is Bank P's figure for 2023.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did Bank P's number of savings accounts grow from 2021 to 2025?

solution.concept: Growth rates over successive years multiply; they do not add
solution.why_others_wrong: 65% adds the four yearly rates; 90.75% confuses the 2025 number of accounts (in lakh) with the growth; 45.2% stops at 2024.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In which year from 2022 to 2025 did Bank Q have the fewest savings accounts?

solution.concept: The graph shows growth rates, not numbers: a positive rate means the number still rose
solution.explanation: Bank Q's accounts: 2022: 50 lakh; 2023: 60; 2024: 57.6; 2025: 64.8. The fewest were in 2022, even though its growth rate (25%) was the highest.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2024 is the only year of decline, but 57.6 lakh is still above 2022's 50 lakh; 2025 has a low growth rate but the most accounts; 2023 has 60 lakh.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: At the end of 2025, 30% of Bank P's savings accounts and 25% of Bank Q's were zero-balance accounts. What percentage of the two banks' combined savings accounts were zero-balance (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Find both banks' 2025 numbers, then take a weighted average of the two percentages
solution.explanation: 2025: Bank P 90.75 lakh, Bank Q 64.8 lakh. Zero-balance: 27.225 + 16.2 = 43.425 lakh out of 155.55 lakh = 27.92%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 27.50% is the simple average of 30% and 25%; 27.78% weights them by the 2021 numbers (50 and 40 lakh); 55.00% adds the two percentages.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many 2BHK flats are occupied by their owners?

solution.concept: 2BHK flats = 5/12 of 240; owners occupy the 70% that are not let out
solution.explanation: 2BHK flats = 5/12 × 240 = 100; 30% (30) are let out, so 70 are owner-occupied.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 is the number let out; 100 is all the 2BHK flats; 60 is the number of 1BHK flats.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many flats in all are let out to tenants?

solution.concept: Apply each type's own percentage to that type's number of flats
solution.explanation: 1BHK: 40% of 60 = 24; 2BHK: 30% of 100 = 30; 3BHK: 25% of 80 = 20. Total let out = 74.
solution.why_others_wrong: 72 applies the 2BHK rate (30%) to all 240 flats; 166 is the number of owner-occupied flats; 76 applies the simple average of the three rates (31⅔%) to all 240 flats.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the total amount the society collects each month (maintenance plus non-occupancy charges)?

solution.concept: Maintenance on all 240 flats, plus 10% extra on the let-out flats only
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹7,80,000 forgets the non-occupancy charge; ₹8,58,000 adds 10% on every flat; ₹7,57,200 subtracts the non-occupancy charge instead of adding it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the total monthly amount paid for the let-out 3BHK flats to that paid for the owner-occupied 1BHK flats?

solution.concept: Each let-out flat pays its maintenance × 1.1; owner-occupied flats pay maintenance only
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 : 4 forgets the 10% non-occupancy charge (90,000 : 72,000); 5 : 9 compares the numbers of flats (20 : 36); 99 : 40 compares the charge for a single flat (4,950 : 2,000).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Next year the maintenance charge rises by 8% for 1BHK flats and by 12% for 2BHK and 3BHK flats, and 6 more 3BHK flats that are now owner-occupied are let out to tenants. Nothing else changes. What will the society's total monthly collection then be?

solution.concept: Recompute each type's charge, then add 10% for each let-out flat at the new charge
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹8,94,144 forgets the 6 newly let-out 3BHK flats; ₹8,68,800 leaves out the non-occupancy charge; ₹9,02,160 raises the 1BHK charge by 12% instead of 8%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the gross NPA ratio of Branch K?

solution.concept: Gross NPA ratio = gross NPAs ÷ gross advances × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 45% misplaces the decimal point; 60% is Branch K's provision coverage (10.8 ÷ 18); 2.7% divides the provisions, not the NPAs, by the advances.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What were the gross advances of Branch L?

solution.concept: Advances = NPAs ÷ (NPA ratio ÷ 100)
solution.explanation: NPAs of ₹15 crore are 5% of advances, so advances = 15 ÷ 0.05 = ₹300 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹75 crore multiplies 15 by 5 instead of dividing by 5%; ₹3,000 crore slips a zero; ₹25 crore uses the 60% coverage (15 ÷ 0.6), which relates provisions to NPAs, not NPAs to advances.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What were the provisions held by Branch N?

solution.concept: Provisions = NPAs × coverage ÷ 100
solution.explanation: Branch N's NPAs are ₹20 crore and its coverage is 80%, so provisions = 0.8 × 20 = ₹16 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹20 crore is the NPA amount itself; ₹4 crore is the uncovered part (20 − 16); ₹200 crore applies 80% to the advances instead of the NPAs.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Taking the five branches together, what was the overall gross NPA ratio (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Fill in the missing advances and NPAs first; the overall ratio is total NPAs ÷ total advances
solution.explanation: Missing values: L's advances 300; M's NPAs 3.2% of 500 = 16; O's NPAs 13.5 ÷ 0.75 = 18 and advances 18 ÷ 0.06 = 300. Totals: advances 400 + 300 + 500 + 250 + 300 = 1,750; NPAs 18 + 15 + 16 + 20 + 18 = 87. Ratio = 87 ÷ 1,750 = 4.97%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.34% is the simple average of the five ratios (4.5, 5, 3.2, 8, 6); 4.76% leaves out Branch O, whose values are missing; 3.50% divides total provisions, not NPAs, by advances.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Net NPAs = gross NPAs − provisions. Which branch had the highest net NPAs as a percentage of its gross advances?

solution.concept: Complete the table, compute net NPAs for each branch, then divide by that branch's advances

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The number of diagonals of an octagon
Quantity II: The number of edges of a cube plus the number of faces of a cube

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Diagonals of an n-sided polygon = n(n − 3)/2
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 8 × 5 ÷ 2 = 20. Quantity II = 12 edges + 6 faces = 18. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' and '≤' come from halving the diagonal count twice (8 × 5 ÷ 4 = 10) or from counting the octagon's diagonals as n(n − 3) ÷ 2 with n = 6 (9).
solution.final_answer: Option B: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: 15% of 15% of 2,000
Quantity II: The square root of 2,209

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Successive percentages multiply; 47² = 2,209
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 0.15 × 0.15 × 2,000 = 45. Quantity II = √2,209 = 47. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' and '≥' come from taking 15% of 15% as 30% (600), or √2,209 as 43.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Average speed (km/h) of a car that covers 120 km at 40 km/h and the next 120 km at 60 km/h
Quantity II: Speed (km/h) of a 300 m long train that passes a signal pole in 20 seconds

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: For equal distances the average speed is the harmonic mean 2ab/(a + b); 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 240 km ÷ (3 h + 2 h) = 48 km/h. Quantity II = 300 ÷ 20 = 15 m/s = 54 km/h. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' and '≥' come from leaving the train's speed in m/s (15), which is then compared with 48 km/h.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The value of x, where x² − 20x + 96 = 0
Quantity II: The value of y, where y² − 26y + 165 = 0

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Find all roots; if one root of I lies between the roots of II, no single relation holds
solution.explanation: I: (x − 8)(x − 12) = 0, so x = 8 or 12. II: (y − 11)(y − 15) = 0, so y = 11 or 15. x = 12 is above y = 11 but below y = 15, and x = 8 is below both. So the relationship cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' uses only x = 12 against y = 11; '≤' and '<' ignore the pair x = 12, y = 11.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Marked price (₹) of an article that costs ₹2,000 and is sold at a 17% profit after a 10% discount
Quantity II: Amount (₹) of ₹2,000 after 3 years at 10% per annum compound interest, compounded annually

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: MP = SP ÷ (1 − discount); compound amount = P(1 + r)ⁿ
solution.explanation: Quantity I: SP = 2,000 × 1.17 = 2,340, so MP = 2,340 ÷ 0.9 = ₹2,600. Quantity II: 2,000 × 1.331 = ₹2,662. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' and '≥' come from comparing the marked price with only the interest in II (₹662) instead of the amount (₹2,662).
solution.final_answer: Option B: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: B's share (₹) of a profit of ₹34,000, if A invests ₹40,000 for 12 months and B invests ₹60,000 for 9 months
Quantity II: Simple interest (₹) on ₹45,000 at 8% per annum for 4½ years

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Profit shares ∝ capital × time; SI = PRT/100
solution.explanation: Quantity I: A 4,80,000, B 5,40,000, ratio 8 : 9, so B gets 34,000 × 9/17 = ₹18,000. Quantity II: 45,000 × 0.08 × 4.5 = ₹16,200. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' and '≤' come from sharing the profit by time alone (12 : 9, so B gets 34,000 × 9/21 ≈ 14,571).
solution.final_answer: Option C: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Volume (cm³) of a hemisphere of radius 6 cm (take π = 22/7)
Quantity II: Volume (cm³) of a cone of base radius 6 cm and height 14 cm (take π = 22/7)

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Hemisphere: ⅔πr³; cone: ⅓πr²h
solution.explanation: Quantity I = ⅔ × 22/7 × 216 = 3,168/7 ≈ 452.57 cm³. Quantity II = ⅓ × 22/7 × 36 × 14 = 528 cm³. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' and '≥' come from using the sphere's 4/3πr³ (905.14) for the hemisphere.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Days taken by A and B together to finish a job that A alone finishes in 18 days and B alone in 24 days
Quantity II: Hours taken to fill a tank by two pipes that fill it in 15 and 20 hours, while a leak that empties the full tank in 60 hours is also open

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Add the rates (subtract the leak's rate) and invert
solution.explanation: Quantity I = 1 ÷ (1/18 + 1/24) = 1 ÷ 7/72 = 72/7 ≈ 10.29 days. Quantity II = 1 ÷ (1/15 + 1/20 − 1/60) = 1 ÷ 6/60 = 10 hours. So Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I < Quantity II' and '≤' come from rounding A and B's joint rate 7/72 up to 1/9, which gives 9 days for Quantity I.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The average of the first 20 multiples of 5
Quantity II: A father's present age (years), if the ratio of the ages of the father and his son is 7 : 3 now and was 3 : 1 eight years ago

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Average of an arithmetic progression = (first + last) ÷ 2; set up the age ratio with a common multiplier
solution.explanation: Quantity I = (5 + 100) ÷ 2 = 52.5. Quantity II: father 7k, son 3k; 7k − 8 = 3(3k − 8) ⇒ 2k = 16 ⇒ k = 8, so the father is 56. So Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' and '≥' come from using the father's age eight years ago (48) in II.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The value of x, where 3ˣ × 9 = 27^(x − 1)
Quantity II: The value of y, where y² − 5y + 6 = 0

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Write every term as a power of 3 and equate exponents
solution.explanation: Quantity I: 3^(x + 2) = 3^(3x − 3), so x + 2 = 3x − 3 and x = 2.5. Quantity II: (y − 2)(y − 3) = 0, so y = 2 or 3. 2.5 is above 2 but below 3, so the relationship cannot be established.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Quantity I > Quantity II' compares 2.5 with y = 2 only; '≤' and '<' compare it with y = 3 only.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the speed of the boat in still water?
I. The boat covers 30 km downstream in 2 hours.
II. The boat's upstream speed is 10 km/h.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Both statements I and II together are needed
Statements I and II together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Still-water speed = (downstream speed + upstream speed) ÷ 2; both speeds are needed
solution.explanation: I gives the downstream speed, 15 km/h, but not the stream's speed. II gives only the upstream speed. Together: (15 + 10) ÷ 2 = 12.5 km/h.
steps: I alone: b + s = 15 (one equation, two unknowns)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' and 'II alone' each give one equation in two unknowns (boat and stream); 'not sufficient even together' misses that the two equations solve directly.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Both statements I and II together are needed

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the area of the circle? (Use π = 22/7.)
I. The circumference of the circle is 44 cm.
II. The diameter of the circle is 14 cm.

options.text: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Both statements I and II together are needed

solution.concept: Any one measurement of a circle fixes its radius, and hence its area
solution.explanation: I: 2πr = 44 ⇒ r = 7 cm ⇒ area = 154 cm² — sufficient. II: r = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 cm ⇒ area 154 cm² — sufficient. Either statement alone answers the question.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' or 'II alone' overlooks that the other statement also fixes the radius; 'both together' assumes the two must be combined.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the profit percentage on the article?
I. The cost price of 12 such articles equals the selling price of 10 of them.
II. The selling price of the article is ₹600.

options.text: Both statements I and II together are needed
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient

solution.concept: A profit percentage needs only the ratio of SP to CP, not the actual prices
solution.explanation: I: 12 CP = 10 SP ⇒ SP/CP = 6/5 ⇒ profit = 20% — sufficient on its own. II gives the selling price but nothing about the cost, so it is not sufficient.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Both together' assumes rupee values are needed, but a percentage needs only the ratio; 'II alone' and 'either' forget that II says nothing about the cost.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: What is the length of the rectangle? (Its length is greater than its breadth.)
I. The area of the rectangle is 180 m².
II. The length exceeds the breadth by 8 m.
III. The perimeter of the rectangle is 56 m.

options.text: Any two of the three statements together are sufficient
Only I and II together are sufficient
Only II and III together are sufficient
All three statements together are necessary

solution.concept: Check every pair: each gives two independent equations in length and breadth
solution.explanation: I + II: l(l − 8) = 180 ⇒ l = 18. I + III: l + b = 28 and lb = 180 ⇒ l, b = 18, 10, and since the length is the longer side, l = 18. II + III: l − b = 8, l + b = 28 ⇒ l = 18. No single statement is enough.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Only I and II' and 'only II and III' each miss that the other pairs also work; 'all three' is more than needed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Any two of the three statements together are sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the two-digit number?
I. Its two digits differ by 3.
II. The number is 4 times the sum of its digits.

options.text: Both statements I and II together are needed
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statements I and II together are not sufficient

solution.concept: List the numbers each statement allows and look for a single common value
solution.explanation: I allows many numbers (14, 41, 25, 52, 36, 63, …). II: 10a + b = 4(a + b) ⇒ b = 2a, giving 12, 24, 36, 48. Together only 36 (digits 3 and 6 differ by 3) remains.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'II alone' leaves four numbers; 'I alone' leaves many; 'not sufficient together' misses that only 36 satisfies both.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both statements I and II together are needed

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the value of x + y, where x and y are real numbers?
I. x² + y² = 25
II. xy = 12

options.text: Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are needed
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient

solution.concept: (x + y)² = x² + y² + 2xy, but a square root has two signs
solution.explanation: Together: (x + y)² = 25 + 24 = 49, so x + y = 7 or −7 (for example x = 3, y = 4 or x = −3, y = −4). Two values remain, so even both statements together are not sufficient.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Both together' takes only the positive root, 7; 'I alone' and 'either' ignore that I alone allows many pairs (e.g. 0 and 5, 3 and 4).
solution.final_answer: Option A: Statements I and II together are not sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: What is the cost price of the article?
I. The article is marked 40% above its cost price.
II. It is sold at a discount of 10% on the marked price.
III. The profit on the sale is ₹338.

options.text: Only I and III together are sufficient
All three statements together are necessary
Only II and III together are sufficient
Any two of the three statements together are sufficient

solution.concept: The profit in rupees fixes the cost only when the profit percentage is known, which needs both I and II
solution.explanation: I + II: SP = 1.4 × 0.9 × CP = 1.26 CP, a 26% profit, but no rupee value. I + III or II + III: the profit percentage is unknown. All three: 0.26 CP = 338 ⇒ CP = ₹1,300.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Only I and III' forgets the discount; 'only II and III' forgets the mark-up; 'any two' assumes the pair I + II is enough, but it gives a percentage, not a rupee value.
solution.final_answer: Option B: All three statements together are necessary
